question:
A 53-year-old male patient attends a routine primary care visit where urinalysis reveals 3+ protein and
1–2 red blood cells per high-power field, with no other abnormalities. He has no symptoms, no relevant
family history, and denies smoking or alcohol use. His vital signs include a temperature of 36.7°C
(98.06°F), blood pressure of 156/71 mm Hg, and a pulse rate of 78/min. Physical examination findings
are unremarkable. What is the next best step in managing this patient’s condition? Answer Choices: (A)
Repeating the urine dipstick test (B) 24-hour urine collection (C) Referring to a nephrologist
immediately (D) Ordering a renal biopsy (E) Performing a kidney ultrasound (F) Prescribing a
low-protein diet (G) Testing for urinary Bence Jones proteins (H) Starting captopril (I) Measuring serum
albumin and creatinine (J) Initiating corticosteroid therapy
 A. Prescribing a low-protein diet
B. Testing for urinary Bence Jones proteins
C. Repeating the urine dipstick test
D. Initiating corticosteroid therapy
E. Performing a kidney ultrasound
F. 24-hour urine collection
G. Referring to a nephrologist immediately
H. Starting captopril
I. Ordering a renal biopsy
J. Measuring serum albumin and creatinine
